substeps.caption: From the VLM to the atomizer: MiR250 1 carries the four charged 5N Al cups, 156.7 g of Al-10Si (Si powder under each plug), to the AMAZEMET rePowder. Four charges is how the lab loads the crucible; its own Al runs were 169-180 g (DAL #159). MiR250 2 comes over from the aisle for the lid.

From the VLM to the atomizer: MiR250 1 carries the four charged 5N Al cups, 156.7 g of Al-10Si (Si powder under each plug), to the AMAZEMET rePowder. Four charges is how the lab loads the crucible; its own Al runs were 169-180 g (DAL #159). MiR250 2 comes over from the aisle for the lid.

Parked, each MiR250 lowers two sprung copper-graphite shoes onto a bonded steel plate set in the floor; its lamp turns green once shoe to shoe and plate to the ground bar both read 1 ohm or less, before any arm moves near the powder (ours, as in the vacuum clip; to be checked by EHS).

Two MiR250 + UR10e units: arm 1 works the furnace's latch and loads the cups, from its right; arm 2 swings the lid, from the front left; in the pour both steer the plate. Each MiR250 carries a 131 kg steel plate, 40 mm thick, on its deck under the cabinet: the weight as low as a top module can carry it, so an arm can pull on the machine without tipping its base (sums in notes/alloy_atomize.md).

The furnace stands rebuilt and at atmosphere, so the machine's pneumatic bolt is back: it locks the latch's lever only while the furnace is pumped or pressurised (AMAZEMET). The lid is held by one over-centre draw latch on the housing's right face: a lever that pivots at its top and hangs over its base, and a wire loop hooked on a keeper on the lid.
Arm 1 takes the lever near its free end, the 2F-85's pads on its two side flanges, 133 mm below the pivot. The lever pivots at its top and hangs flat over its base (T4 5:35.5).

Arm 1 lets the lever back to 42 deg, where it rests on the slack loop, whose bar sits on the keeper's hook again; then it lets go. The lid is still hooked on: the loop has to come off the keeper first.

The cups go in with a loading tong: in effect a pair of long fingers for the 2F-85. Two flat spring-steel bars slide past each other; each ends in a jaw at the bottom and a handle half at the top, and each handle half is pinned to one of the gripper's fingertips, so each jaw moves with its finger. A thin flexure at the top holds the halves square and the jaws open when the tong is left alone. Ours, not built.
The fingertips' pins go into the handle halves and the gripper closes just onto them: the jaws stay open, 1.6 mm clear of a cup's sides each. Its wrist camera looks down past the tong.

Latched. The lever's pull is not measured: about 100 N, 200 N for a stiff one (cover latches of this kind). MiR250 1, with its 131 kg plate, would tip at 783 N and slide at 952 N (435 and 539 N without the plate). The bolt locks the lever at the first pump-down.
MiR250 2 goes round to the left of the chamber's door, where the plate's landing stage is (ours): in the pour, both arms steer the plate. MiR250 1 waits at the right.

The first pump-down starts. As the furnace leaves atmosphere, the machine's bolt comes in through the latch's base and the lever: the lid can't be opened under vacuum or pressure (AMAZEMET, install call).

Cut open at the furnace axis; the two back cups are cut through their own axes. Three cycles of pumping down to 4×10⁻¹ mbar and back-filling with 5N argon take the oxygen under 50 ppm. On each pump-down the air under the plugs leaves through their 1/16 in vents (#104).

The stack under the charge was built by the two arms between runs (the turnaround, next): arm 1 holds the graphite crucible still from above with its three-jaw crucible gripper while arm 2, through the chamber's door, threads the thin graphite nut on from below with a socket key, "snug but never forced" (the lab's SOP), at a torque set from bench trials. notes/atom_crucible.md

The 10 kW, 7 kHz coil heats the graphite and the graphite the charge. The Type N thermocouple sits in the crucible wall, so the metal lags its reading. The cups glow, then slump into a pool round the rod (Al-10Si is liquid above about 595 °C; a 750 °C hold is assumed).

Real footage, Oct 27 2026, through the furnace port: the four bronze pieces stand round the sealing rod and glow (youtu.be/2brsz-90seg, DAL #219). 630 bronze at 1300 °C, not Al-10Si.
A few minutes on, the pieces sink into their own melt round the rod (2brsz-90seg, about 4:36; at 3:55 Gage says "It's melting in right now").
The charge fully molten, a bright pool round the sealing rod (2brsz-90seg, DAL #219).
Before the pour, MiR250 1 comes round to the front left of the chamber's door, where MiR250 2 already waits: the plate is steered during the pour.

Steering the plate (ours). A landing stage between the door and the stack's housing, sealed by a bellows, moves the stack under argon: its u knob slides the stack along its axis, so the stream lands nearer to or further from the plate's hole; its v knob moves it across, under the stream. Each knob is a lead screw, 8 mm a turn, with a brake that holds it when let go. Arm 2 takes the u knob, arm 1 the v knob, and both hold on through the pour.

Vibration on, then 200 mbar of argon over-pressure on the furnace: the pour runs on the pressure, not the melt's weight (#222). Sealing rod up: the stream falls through the nozzle onto the vibrating plate, 75 mm from its hole, where the lab sets it (#261).

Droplets fly off the plate, freeze in the argon and run down the cone into the container. In the corner, a schematic of what the melt-stream cameras (DAL PR 189: the door's sight glass and the front view port) measure: where the stream meets the plate, in mm, the plate's own size for scale. The landing drifts as the nozzle wears and the plate erodes; the cell acts past 1 mm.
Real footage, Oct 27 2026, through the view port: the bronze jet lands on the tip of the W-coated carbon-fibre plate and atomizes (2brsz-90seg). 91 % of the 1,080 g became usable powder (DAL #219).

1.4 mm too far down the plate and 1.2 mm off its middle: arm 2 turns the u knob an eighth of a turn (the stack slides 1 mm in, the landing 1 mm nearer the hole) and arm 1 the v knob an eighth (the plate 1 mm across). The stream keeps falling where it was; the plate moves under it.
The pour goes on, and so does the drift. Each correction is an eighth or a quarter of a turn of a knob, now and then: the arms hold on, but don't move most of the time.

2 mm and 1.4 mm off: the u knob a quarter of a turn (2 mm), the v knob three sixteenths (1.5 mm). Nothing is opened and the argon stays in: the bellows takes the movement. Ours, to check with AMAZEMET (the stack's seal at the door, the transducer's cable and cooling air, whether the plate may move while it vibrates).
The powder collects in the container under the chamber's valve, still under argon. At the Oct 27 bronze run's yield, 91 % usable (DAL #219), the four cups make about 143 g of powder.
The crucible runs empty; vibration and the coil off, the sealing rod down.

How much powder: the four cups make about 26 g of the MIDI's 20-63 um cut, at the Oct 27 run's 17 % under 63 um (DAL #219). The crucible takes much more: filled as on Oct 27, about 385 g of Al (65 g of the cut), and the 400 cm³ one about 684 g (116 g). A 440 g MIDI build then takes 17, 7 or 4 runs.
Done: the powder, not yet sieved, is on the MiR250 in front of the rePowder. Next: the sieving cell and the printer.
